rounds.proof_sketch: N=2048, TILE_SIZE=32. gridDim.x=(2048+31)/32=64. Maximum col=63*32+31=2047. Since max(col)=2047<N=2048, both 'col<N' and 'col<=N' evaluate to TRUE for all thread columns. The mutation would only differ if col==N=2048, but this value is never reached.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the write-back guard from 'col < N' to 'col <= N'. However, with the fixed dimensions (N=2048), the grid is configured with gridDim.x = 64 blocks (since 2048/32=64 exactly). The maximum column index any thread can compute is (gridDim.x-1)*TILE_SIZE + (TILE_SIZE-1) = 63*32+31 = 2047. Since the maximum col (2047) is strictly less than N (2048), the original condition 'col < N' is always TRUE, and the mutated condition 'col <= N' is also always TRUE. The boundary case col==N that would distinguish the two conditions is architecturally unreachable given these fixed dimensions.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation would only be observable if N were not divisible by TILE_SIZE (e.g., N=2049), causing some threads to have col values equal to N. With N=2048 exactly divisible by 32, the mutation is semantically equivalent.
rounds.recommendations: When testing relational operator mutations in tiled GPU kernels, verify whether the boundary condition (e.g., col==N) is actually reachable given the tile size and problem dimensions. Mutations to boundary guards are only killable when the grid/block configuration allows threads to reach the exact boundary value. For dimensions that are exact multiples of tile size, such mutations become equivalent and require configuration changes (different shapes) to distinguish.
